title: Vance in Texas, 11 days of posts

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: JD Vance told a man at a Texas rally who said he loved him that he is the vice president, not James Talarico.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Several outlets report that Vance said this at an Oct. 13, 2026 campaign rally in Tyler, Texas. CBS Austin reports that 
a man in the audience yelled "I love you," and Vance replied, "I love you too, sir... I'm the vice president, not James Talarico."
 The Advocate and the Washington Blade both cite C-SPAN video of the exchange. The Washington Blade says the rally was 
part of Vance's campaigning for Ken Paxton
. The quote, the setting (Texas rally) and the attribution all match the claim as worded. Vance also added "in a totally platonic way," and critics read the remark as a joke about Talarico's sexuality. The claim leaves out that context, but nothing it says is wrong.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: JD Vance announced that the Trump administration is using the Defense Production Act to expand a key refinery in Tyler, Texas.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Several outlets report that Vance made this announcement at a Tyler, Texas campaign rally for Ken Paxton on Tuesday, Oct 13, 2026. The Tyler Morning Telegraph and Reuters-based coverage quote him saying 
the Trump administration, working with the refinery at Delek, "has used the Defense Production Act and we are gonna expand the refinery right here in Tyler, Texas."
 The Washington Examiner also 
reports that he announced Trump is invoking the Defense Production Act to expand the Delek refinery in Tyler
. This matches the claim's wording. Reporting does note that 
he gave no cost or planned capacity increase
, and that the details of the DPA use have not been fully disclosed. That is a caveat about missing detail and does not contradict the claim, which only says Vance announced it. I did not find a primary document such as a DPA order or a White House release.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: James Talarico said that racism is a virus white people spread simply by virtue of their skin color.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Talarico did tweet this on May 8, 2020, after Ahmaud Arbery's death. 
He wrote that "White skin gives me and every white American immunity from the virus," but that "we spread it wherever we go—through our words, our actions, and our systems." He added that "we don't have to be showing symptoms—like a white hood or a Confederate flag—to be contagious."
 (Fox News; Daily Caller; Headline USA). 
Fox News reports he defended the tweets at SXSW, saying they were taken out of context.
 The "virus" metaphor and the attribution to white Americans are accurate. But in the text he quoted, skin color is what makes white people immune to the harm. He said the spreading happens through words, actions and systems, so "simply by virtue of their skin color" is the claim's own gloss. It is a hostile reading of the tweet, not what the tweet says. I found no record of him saying racism spreads merely because of skin color. I also found no connection to Vance in these results, and the tweet was published by Talarico himself, so the attribution is not in doubt.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: JD Vance implied that James Talarico is gay.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The quote is well documented. At the Oct. 13, 2026 Tyler rally, Vance answered a man in the crowd who shouted that he loved him. 
He said, "I love you, too, Sir! In a totally platonic way — to be clear. I'm the vice president, not James Talarico."
 Newsweek's account of the rally includes the same exchange. 
CNN's analysis says Vance "made a joke that implied James Talarico is gay."
 
CNN's Jake Tapper described it as insinuating that Talarico is gay.
 HuffPost, via Yahoo, and the Advocate use the same reading. Vance did not say Talarico is gay, and I found no statement from him or his office explaining what he meant. "Implied" is therefore an interpretation of a joke, but it is how several established outlets characterize it, and the wording is accurate as a description of the remark. 
Tapper also noted a separate line in which Vance referred to Talarico's comments on "trans children" and then mused about his "internet search history."

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: JD Vance suggested James Talarico's internet search history is something people would not want to see, and doubled down on it.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Reporting from Forbes, Fox News and others shows Vance made the remark and then repeated it. At a Tuesday (Oct 13, 2026) rally in Tyler, 
he said "You gotta wonder what the internet search history of a man like that looks like," and added that listeners don't want to find out.
 Asked about it by a reporter, 
he said people who say such things "tend to have some unusual search histories," then added "Maybe he doesn't. Just guessing. But I wouldn't want to see it."
 Fox News itself described this as Vance 
"doubling down on his comments about James Talarico's internet search history."
 Forbes says 
he repeated the line later that day.
 The sources differ on the order of the two remarks, but both happened. The claim is accurate as worded. Vance himself conceded he was speculating, and Forbes noted that 
no evidence or credible allegations of misconduct have surfaced against Talarico.
 The claim doesn't say otherwise.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: JD Vance's remark about not being James Talarico was a masterful line.
The Talarico campaign has not explained where James Talarico was for two weeks.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The campaign did explain the absence. Talarico and spokesman J.T. Ennis said he was home in Austin with the flu. Talarico told a Sept. 30 event he had gone to urgent care in Dallas, and he later said he saw his primary care physician (
CBS News
). The campaign also gave security-camera images to the New York Times and CBS News. 
CBS reported they show him at home every day from Oct. 1 to Oct. 8.
 
FactCheck.org said the Times verified he was at his house by reviewing the time-stamped images.
 Another Talarico stop, in New York City on Sept. 28, was also reported (
Scripps
). The Ohio mental-health-facility story was a rumor with no evidence behind it, and 
the Lindner Center of Hope said Talarico "has never received treatment" there.
 Critics' complaints are narrower: 
the Times was allowed to inspect the images on the condition that they not be published
, and 
the campaign reportedly declined a Fox 7 Zoom "proof-of-life" interview
. The claim as worded, that the campaign "has not explained" where he was, is contradicted by the record, though some people dispute how complete the explanation is.

clusters.text: A Senate candidate with the flu would take off three days at most, so a two-week absence suggests a medical emergency.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: A crowd gathered at JD Vance's rally in Tyler, Texas shortly before the program started.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Vance did hold a rally at Tyler Pounds Regional Airport on Oct. 13, 2026. 
KLTV reported he drew a crowd of supporters and critics
, and 
the Tyler Morning Telegraph described him speaking in front of a crowd outside a hangar
. The wording closely tracks a viral post by the "FactPost" X account. 
That post was captioned "The crowd at JD Vance's rally in Tyler, Texas minutes out from the start of the program."
 
Newsweek says the photo showed rows of white folding chairs, many unoccupied.
 
Trump's campaign operation disputed it
, and 
Newsweek says the available material doesn't establish how many people attended
. 
Doors opened at 8 a.m. and the event began at 10 a.m.
, and 
Vance took the podium shortly before noon
. So I found no independent confirmation of the crowd's size or composition at the moment the photo was taken. The claim says a crowd "gathered", but the only source for the "shortly before the program" detail is a photo that mainly shows empty seats, and the size of the crowd at that moment is disputed. The claim is therefore misleading as worded.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: JD Vance said James Talarico has a weird focus on transgender kids and drag queens.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Several outlets report that Vance said this on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, before leaving for Texas to campaign for Ken Paxton. A reporter asked what he meant by saying he "wouldn't want to see" Talarico's search history. Vance answered that Talarico is "just a guy who shows a weird focus on transgender kids and drag queens." 
Forbes reported the quote
, and 
TheWrap reported it too
. The Fox News post and Joe.My.God's transcript carry the same wording. The wording of the claim matches the quote, and the attribution and the target are both correct. Forbes also notes that 
no evidence or credible allegations of misconduct have surfaced against Talarico
, and Vance conceded he was guessing. That context goes beyond what the claim says, but it doesn't make the claim inaccurate.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: JD Vance is rallying in Texas with Ken Paxton and other Republicans ahead of the midterms.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Several outlets report that Vance held a midterm campaign rally in Tyler, Texas, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. The Tyler Morning Telegraph reports that 
Paxton, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, House Speaker Dustin Burrows, Reps. Van Duyne, Moran and Gill, Comptroller candidate Don Huffines and congressional candidate Trever Nehls joined Vance
. The Washington Times describes it as 
a campaign rally for several Republican candidates on the November midterm ballot
, and Fox 7 Austin reports that Vance 
endorsed Paxton and criticized Talarico ahead of the Nov. 3 election
. This was not Vance's only Texas stop. Texas Scorecard notes 
it was his second campaign appearance in Texas in under two weeks, after Brownsville and Harlingen on Sept. 30
. The Hill reports Paxton missed that earlier South Texas rally. The present-tense claim is accurate for the Tyler rally, where Paxton and other Republicans were present, and it is a fair summary of Vance's wider Texas campaigning.

clusters.text: A large crowd, hundreds of people, attended JD Vance's East Texas rally.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The rally did happen. It was held in Tyler on Oct. 13 and hosted by the Trump 47 Committee. The Tyler Morning Telegraph reported that the outdoor venue 
eventually grew to a standing-room only crowd
. KLTV published photos of long lines and, per Newsweek, reported that the event was 
"well attended."
 So "large crowd" has local reporting behind it. However, no source I found gives an attendance figure or an official estimate. Newsweek said 
available material from the Texas rally does not establish how many people attended
. Photos of sparse seating shortly before the start were disputed by the Trump War Room's video, and critics online guessed at figures such as 150 (Irish Star). "Hundreds" is plausible for a standing-room-only crowd, but I can't confirm it. The overall characterization fits the reporting, but the specific number isn't documented.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: Ken Paxton has refused to answer questions about why he won't debate.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Reporting does show that Paxton's campaign has been unresponsive on debates. Houston Public Media reported that 
Paxton's campaign has not responded to repeated requests for comment about whether he ever intends to debate
. KXAN reported that 
Paxton has yet to publicly acknowledge the debate requests
. The claim is too absolute, though. When Fox News host Johnny Jones asked whether a debate was in the works, Paxton did answer (Mediaite, Yahoo). 
He said his campaign had been working on it for months and "we can never quite work out the details because he always wants something we can't do."
 The Talarico campaign disputed that account (
saying Paxton had "ignored every single attempt"
), but the dispute is about whether his answer was true, not whether he gave one. His spokesperson also said in July, 
"of course we're going to debate."
 The accurate version is that Paxton has declined or ignored debate invitations and campaign press inquiries about them, while giving at least one on-the-record explanation. "Refused to answer questions" overstates that.

clusters.event: Vance rallies for Paxton in Tyler
clusters.text: Ken Paxton's net worth has increased 7,000% since he entered public office.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The 7,000% figure traces to a Talarico campaign ad. 
Fox's Jacqui Heinrich asked Paxton about an ad saying his "net worth has increased 7,000%."
 The Texas Democratic Party, summarizing a New York Times story, phrased it more loosely: 
his wealth "has increased by up to 7,000%" while in elected office.
 I could not find the Times text itself, so the 7,000% figure is not confirmed there. The underlying records point to a large rise but not a fixed percentage. 
The Wall Street Journal, working from subpoenaed documents, found Paxton had under $175,000 in assets when he entered public service in 2002.
 That is a figure for assets, not net worth. 
Bank statements put his net worth at about $5.4 million before his blind trust was created.
 
Forbes estimates he is now worth roughly $13 million.
 Those inputs give roughly 3,000% to 7,000% or more, depending on which figures you pair. One X post attributes a 4,000% figure to the WSJ (
"Ken Paxton's net worth has increased 4,000% while in public office, per WSJ"
), but I did not find that in the WSJ reporting itself. Current net worth is also uncertain.
